A profitable company earns 95% of its revenue from a single flagship product whose core market is mature and growing at under 2% per year. The board is concerned about concentration risk, but two previous diversification attempts failed because they strayed too far from the company's capabilities. The company has strong cash reserves, a loyal customer base, and deep expertise in its niche.

Design a diversification strategy that reduces single-product dependency without repeating past failures. Identify what kinds of adjacencies to pursue, how to evaluate them against the company's actual capabilities, whether to build, buy, or partner, and how to stage investment so early failures do not endanger the core business.

agentResponses.content:
Let me start somewhere slightly to the side of the question, if you'll indulge me.

Two attempts failed because they "strayed too far from capabilities." That's the diagnosis on the record. I'd want to hold it loosely. In my experience the stated cause and the real cause rarely sit in the same room. Worth asking, quietly, of the people who were actually in those ventures: were they starved of attention, or drowned in it? Were they held to the flagship's margin profile in year two? Did they report to someone whose bonus depended on the core? If any of that rings true, then the problem wasn't distance from capability — it was that the core business was allowed to be the parent, and parents tend to smother.

I mention it because the answer changes what you build. If it's genuinely capability distance, you fix that with better screening. If it's governance, better screening won't save you.

**On what "adjacent" ought to mean here**

The instinct is to think in terms of products and markets. I'd suggest thinking in terms of what actually travels. You have three or four assets that are portable and probably underexploited:

The customer relationship, and specifically the *permission* it carries. A loyal base in a niche will let you sell them things you don't currently sell them — but only within a boundary they've drawn, and they've never told you where it is. That boundary is the single most valuable unmapped thing you own.

The channel and installed base. Whatever it costs a competitor to reach these people, you've already paid.

Deep technical expertise in a niche. Narrow, yes. But narrow expertise is often narrow only in application, not in nature.

And whatever you know about your customers' behaviour that nobody outside can see.

Now — the interesting move. "95% of revenue from one product" can be softened along more than one axis, and the product axis is the hardest one. Before you go looking for a second product, I'd look at whether the flagship can carry more revenue *models*: consumables, service contracts, software layers, financing, data or benchmarking, training, certification. Same customer, same trust, same problem. What you're doing is turning a transaction into a relationship, and a mature 2% market into a share-of-wallet question rather than a growth question. It doesn't fully solve concentration risk — the revenue still depends on the same product's presence — but it buys margin, recurring cash, and time, and it teaches you how to sell something new to someone who already trusts you. That's not a trivial lesson to learn cheaply.

Then, in rough order of how many unknowns you're taking on at once:

*Same customer, different need.* Something else in their workflow that sits next to what you sell. One unknown: the new offering. The customer, channel and brand permission are all known quantities.

*Same capability, different customer.* Your technical expertise pointed at an adjacent vertical. One unknown, but a harder one, because you'll be a stranger there and specialists will be waiting.

*Same asset, repurposed.* Licensing, data products, using your channel to carry someone else's goods. Low capital, low glory, occasionally very high return.

Anything requiring two leaps at once — new customer *and* new capability — I'd rule out, not because it can't work but because you can't learn from it. When it fails you won't know which leap killed it.

**How I'd screen, without building a bureaucracy around it**

A simple discipline, and I'd resist the urge to make it elaborate: for each candidate, list every capability required to win. Not to enter — to *win*, against whoever is already there. Mark each one owned, borrowable, buyable, or absent. If more than one falls in "absent," it's a different company's opportunity.

Second question, and I think it's the more revealing one: if a customer who trusts us completely for X were told we now do Y, would they nod or would they blink? You can find this out for the price of a few dozen conversations. It is remarkable how rarely anyone asks.

Third: if this fails, will we know why, and how fast? Cheap information is the actual product of early-stage diversification. Ventures that fail illegibly are worse than ventures that fail fast.

And a fourth I'd keep to myself and apply anyway: does anyone genuinely want to run this, or are we assigning it? Assigned ventures die.

**Build, buy, partner — mostly a question of what you're short of**

Build where the missing thing is only effort, and where the capability itself becomes the moat. Slow, but you keep the learning.

Partner where you're short of *knowledge* and don't yet know if you want to own the position. Distribution partnerships, white-labelling someone else's product through your channel, joint development — these are option purchases dressed as commercial agreements. They're the cheapest way to test whether your customers will buy a category from you at all. If it works, you've learned what to build or buy. If not, you've spent very little and no one need make a speech about it.

Buy where you're short of *time or access* and the target is small enough to absorb without the core reorganising itself around the acquisition. Small teams already selling something to your customer base are the sweet spot — you're buying a validated proposition and people who've done it, and you're the natural distributor. I'd be sceptical of anything transformative. Large acquisitions have a way of turning the periphery into the centre of gravity, and then the core starts serving the venture rather than funding it.

One thing I'd avoid: buying capability you don't understand well enough to evaluate. That's how the previous two probably went, if I had to guess.

**Staging, which is really about protecting the core from your own enthusiasm**

Fund from cash flow, not from reserves. Pick a fraction of annual operating cash — some choose a tenth, some more — and treat it as the annual option budget. The reserves stay untouched, because their job is to make the flagship unassailable and to let you move fast when something real appears. A diversification programme that can impair the balance sheet has already failed regardless of outcome.

Run several small things rather than one large thing. Three or four bets at a size where any single failure is an expensive quarter, not an event. You're buying lottery tickets in a lottery where you get to see the numbers partway through.

Gate on evidence, not revenue. Early on, the question isn't "is this profitable" — nothing is, at that size — it's "did we learn what we said we'd learn." Write the kill criteria before the money goes out, when everyone is still capable of thinking clearly, and make them specific enough that they can't be argued around later. The commitment escalation problem is the real enemy here, and the only defence is a decision made in advance by people who weren't yet invested.

Keep them structurally separate. Own P&L, own hiring, own cadence, judged against their own milestones, and explicitly not against core margins. Borrowing from the core should be deliberate and priced — channel access yes, shared overhead reluctantly, shared management attention almost never. And whoever oversees them should have no stake in the flagship's numbers.

Then let the survivors have real money. The staging is only worth something if the graduation is decisive; a portfolio of permanently small experiments is just an expensive hobby.

**On expectations**

If the ambition is stated as "reduce the flagship to half our revenue," someone will chase scale and you'll get a third failure. Getting to seventy-five or eighty percent over five to seven years, with a second business that genuinely works and a services layer that compounds, would be a considerable achievement — and it would materially change what the board is worried about.

Meanwhile the flagship should be defended and invested in without apology. A 2% market with a loyal base and deep expertise is a very good thing to own. It's the engine that pays for the optionality. The mistake would be to treat maturity as a reason for neglect — that's the failure mode nobody sees coming, because everyone's looking at the new ventures.

One last thought, offered lightly. Your customers already know what they wish you sold them. They've probably mentioned it more than once, to someone in sales, who filed it. I'd start there before I started with a consultant's market map.
